questions.article: Navigating the New Year with Purpose and Wisdom
questions.q: What does the article say is needed for a new year to be truly better than the last?
options: Honest self-assessment – taking stock of what was gained and lost, and planning from it
Yes. Hope alone is not enough.
Advice from many people
Not quite. The article says: Honest self-assessment – taking stock of what was gained and lost, and planning from it.
Forgetting the past year altogether
Not quite. The article says: Honest self-assessment – taking stock of what was gained and lost, and planning from it.
A larger celebration
Not quite. The article says: Honest self-assessment – taking stock of what was gained and lost, and planning from it.
questions.rationale: “A truly successful person is one who conducts a continuous self-evaluation, taking stock of what was gained and lost in the preceding year.”

questions.article: Navigating the New Year with Purpose and Wisdom
questions.q: Which practical tool, recommended by Maulana Wahiduddin Khan, does the article suggest for this self-accounting?
options: Keeping a diary
Right. A record of one’s experiences becomes a guide for growth.
Hiring an adviser
Not quite. The article says: Keeping a diary.
Making public resolutions
Not quite. The article says: Keeping a diary.
Reading last year’s newspapers
Not quite. The article says: Keeping a diary.
questions.rationale: “Maulana Wahiduddin Khan advocated the use of diaries as a means to cultivate intellectual skills.”

questions.q: The article says there are only two ways of living. What are they?
options: A public life and a private life
Not quite. The article says: A self-oriented life and a God-oriented life.
A rich life and a poor life
Not quite. The article says: A self-oriented life and a God-oriented life.
A self-oriented life and a God-oriented life
Yes. There is no third way.
A busy life and a quiet life
Not quite. The article says: A self-oriented life and a God-oriented life.
questions.rationale: “There are two ways of living in this world. One is a self-oriented life, the other a God-oriented one.”

questions.article: The Challenges of the Later Era
questions.q: The article discusses a saying of the Prophet about people who speak fine words and recite the Quran while their faith stays shallow. What danger does it warn of?
options: The decline of public speaking
Not quite. The article says: Performative religiosity – outward show and eloquence winning prominence without depth or wisdom.
Performative religiosity – outward show and eloquence winning prominence without depth or wisdom
Well read. Modern media make this easier.
A shortage of speakers
Not quite. The article says: Performative religiosity – outward show and eloquence winning prominence without depth or wisdom.
Too much study of religion
Not quite. The article says: Performative religiosity – outward show and eloquence winning prominence without depth or wisdom.
questions.rationale: “This can be seen as a warning against the danger of performative religiosity, where outward appearances do not reflect the depth of one’s faith.”

questions.article: Role of Prophets in Shaping Human Destiny
questions.q: Other creatures follow their nature. Why, according to the article, do human beings need guidance through a Prophet?
options: They are weaker than other creatures
Not quite. The article says: They have free will and must find their own code of conduct, but their knowledge is limited.
They have no ability to choose
Not quite. The article says: They have free will and must find their own code of conduct, but their knowledge is limited.
They have free will and must find their own code of conduct, but their knowledge is limited
Correct. What is inborn in others is given to man from outside.
They live shorter lives
Not quite. The article says: They have free will and must find their own code of conduct, but their knowledge is limited.
questions.rationale: “Human limitations in knowledge necessitate external guidance, and the very need for the Prophet’s guidance underscores its inevitability.”

questions.article: Role of Prophets in Shaping Human Destiny
questions.q: By what standard does the article say a life plan should be judged?
options: By how quickly it was made
Not quite. The article says: By its results – a plan that yields positive outcomes is sound.
By how ambitious it sounds
Not quite. The article says: By its results – a plan that yields positive outcomes is sound.
By its results – a plan that yields positive outcomes is sound
Yes. Not by an ideal standard alone.
By how many people approve of it
Not quite. The article says: By its results – a plan that yields positive outcomes is sound.
questions.rationale: “True wisdom resides in assessing actions in light of their results, thereby determining their efficacy and appropriateness.”

questions.q: A man pricked by a rose bush blames the thorns or the gardener. What does the article say was his real mistake?
options: Choosing the wrong flower
Not quite. The article says: His own haste – thorns and flowers together are a law of nature, part of the test.
His own haste – thorns and flowers together are a law of nature, part of the test
Right. No one succeeds by opposing the natural order.
Trusting the gardener
Not quite. The article says: His own haste – thorns and flowers together are a law of nature, part of the test.
Entering the garden at all
Not quite. The article says: His own haste – thorns and flowers together are a law of nature, part of the test.
questions.rationale: “The man’s mistake lies in his impatience, for no one can triumph by opposing the natural order.”

questions.q: What lesson does Dr Nidhi Patel, a farmer’s daughter who topped her university, draw from her own journey?
options: Not to believe in a quick fix, but to build a goal “brick by brick”
Yes. An “incentive spoon” in place of a silver one.
That success depends on family wealth
Not quite. The article says: Not to believe in a quick fix, but to build a goal “brick by brick”.
That awards matter most
Not quite. The article says: Not to believe in a quick fix, but to build a goal “brick by brick”.
That talent needs no effort
Not quite. The article says: Not to believe in a quick fix, but to build a goal “brick by brick”.
questions.rationale: “My learning: Don’t believe in quick fix. Believe in making your goal come true brick by brick.”

questions.q: What does the article name as the root of fanatical violence?
options: Love for one’s own group swelling into intense enmity towards others
Exactly. The remedy is acceptance of differences.
Lack of weapons
Not quite. The article says: Love for one’s own group swelling into intense enmity towards others.
Indifference to one’s group
Not quite. The article says: Love for one’s own group swelling into intense enmity towards others.
Too much education
Not quite. The article says: Love for one’s own group swelling into intense enmity towards others.
questions.rationale: “When love for their own group or organization escalates into an intense enmity towards others, a dangerous mindset takes hold.”

questions.q: Ibn Rawaha said, “Let us come together to increase faith.” What understanding of faith lay behind his words?
options: Faith cannot change in either direction
Not quite. The article says: Faith is like a growing tree – reciting the creed is only the beginning, and remembrance keeps increasing it.
Faith is like a growing tree – reciting the creed is only the beginning, and remembrance keeps increasing it
Well reasoned. Like an ocean that is never filled.
Faith is complete once the creed is recited
Not quite. The article says: Faith is like a growing tree – reciting the creed is only the beginning, and remembrance keeps increasing it.
Faith belongs only to the Companions
Not quite. The article says: Faith is like a growing tree – reciting the creed is only the beginning, and remembrance keeps increasing it.
questions.rationale: “When we remember God, our faith increases… to the latter, kalimah recitation was only the beginning.”
